"RESOLUTION, Proposing an Amendment to the Constitution of Maine to Specify the Qualifications of Electors in State and Local Elections"
'
Good morning Senator Hickman, Representative Supica, and members of the Joint Standing
Committee On Veterans and Legal Affairs. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today. My name
is Representative Billy Bob Faulkingham, and I serve as the House Republican Leader. I represent House District 12, which includes the towns of Franklin, Gouldsboro, Hancock, Sorrento, Sullivan,
Winter Harbor, and Steuben. l'm here to speak in support of LD 1437- "RESOLUTlON, Proposing an Amendment to the Constitution of Maine to Specify the Qualifications of Electors in State and Local
EIections."
This proposed amendment would make it clear that voting in Maine's state, county, and municipal
elections is reserved exclusively for United States citizens. While Maine's Constitution already
restricts voting to U.S. citizens, this amendment would state unambiguously that the fundamental right to vote in our state, county and municipal elections remains reserved for those who are citizens
of the United States.
The integrity of our electoral system depends on well-defined qualifications for voters. While the Maine Constitution currently assumes that voters are U.S. citizens, it does not explicitly state that
only citizens may vote in state, county or local elections. That omission leaves a potential legal and
political gap.
This proposal:
0 Preserves the integrity of elections: Restricting voting to U.S. citizens ensures that only those
with a legal and permanent stake in the country's future help decide its leaders and laws.
0 Reflects national legal standards: Federal elections already require U.S. citizenship to vote;
aligning state and local elections with this standard promotes consistency and reduces
confusion.
0 Protects the value of citizenship: Limiting voting rights to citizens reinforces the significance and responsibilities of becoming a naturalized American.
0 Reduces administrative complexity: A clear rule requiring citizenship simplifies voter
registration processes and verification efforts for election officials.

0 Builds public confidence in election outcomes: Citizens-only voting policies can help maintain trust in the democratic process by addressing concerns about election security and eligibility.
By endorsing LD 1437, the Legislature would provide voters the chance to enshrine in the Maine Constitution what has long been a fundamental democratic principle: that voting is a right and privilege of citizenship. This is not a partisan issue, it's a constitutional and civic one.
ln closing, LD 1437 is about protecting the integrity of Maine's elections, preserving the civic meaning of citizenship, and aligning our constitutional language with both our legal practices and public
expectations. By supporting this resolution, we empower the people of Maine to affirm that voting in
our elections is a right reserved for citizens of the United States, as clearly intended by our constitutional framework.
Thank you for your time, and l'm happy to take any questions.
Respectfully,

To the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs, I offer my thanks for taking the time to allow me to support LD 1437, RESOLUTION, Proposing an
Amendment to the Constitution ofMaine to Speczfil the Qualifications ofElectors in State
and Local Elections. My name is Donny Ardell, and I represent House District 6.
Why limit civil engagement to U.S. citizens? I have professional experience with U.S. Immigration law, married into a family of immigrants, and my family and I lived in other countries as part of my work; as a result, I understand the issue, personally, from several sides. In my residence in those countries, I never expected to be able to be involved in civil life there, in the same Way my wife's family, until they became proudly naturalized
citizens of the U.S., had any expectation to be involved in civil life here. They understood that, until they became fully committed to American life through citizenship,
they were subject to the laws created by those who Were, in the same way I never expected to have a political voice as an American in Saudi Arabia or Yemen, and accepted that I was subject to the laws of their society.
Foreign nationals residing in Maine can choose to fully engage in civil life here by fully crossing the threshold and becoming U.S. citizens. The path to U.S. citizenship for foreign nationals with sufficient visa status and residency time involves an interview to verify eligibility, and a brief test of English language proficiency and basic American history and civics. These communication and knowledge requirements, though rudimentary, are important for the foreign-born voter to show their knowledge and
understanding of what our government structure is, how the three branches interact, and
what their civil rights are.
And if the argument is made that the naturalization process is too difficult or expensive,
programs exist with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services to reduce or defray some or all of the application fee for large and low-income family groups, and policy to waive the language requirement for seniors exists. Clearly, U.S citizenship is attainable.
Additionally, creating a citizenship requirement for voting simplifies balloting and ballot distribution, creating a system less prone to error, confusion, or expensive and time-
consuming ballot recounts.

House District 6

In closing, while I firmly believe in the extension of the U.S. Bill of Rights, and the Maine Declaration of Rights, to all persons present, civic engagement in the voting booth is different, in that it expects both a citizenship and committed residency requirement. As a result, I ask you, as members of this important committee, to act as wise and faithful gatekeepers of civil life in Maine, to trust Maine voters to have a voice and decide if they want committed, U.S. citizen electors to determine matters important to them in their communities at the county, municipal, and local level.
The question at this stage is this: "Do the members of Veterans and Legal Affairs
committee favor allowing Mainers to decide who is eligible to vote in their elections?" It
is my hope the committee can see the wisdom of placing that trust in Mainers. Thank
you.
Thank you,
Donald J. Ardell
State Representative
House District 6

Testimony in Support of LD 175 & 1437: "RESOLUTION, Proposing an Amendment to the Constitution of Maine to Ensure That
Only Citizens of the United States May Participate in Elections" & "RESOLUTION, Proposing an Amendment to the Constitution of Maine to Specify the Qualifications of
Electors in State and Local Elections"
Senator Hickman, Representative Supica, and the distinguished members of the Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs, my name is Harris Van Pate, and I serve as policy analyst for Maine Policy Institute. Maine Policy is a free market think tank, a nonpartisan, non-profit organization that advocates for individual liberty and economic freedom in Maine. Thank you for the opportunity to testify in strong support of LDs 175 and 1437.
The foundation of any democracy rests on the principle that its elections are conducted by and for those legally bound to its laws and institutions. The right to vote is not only a mechanism of self-expression but a responsibility that should be exclusively reserved for United States citizens. These bills reaffirm this principle and clarify our state Constitution to ensure that the integrity of Maine's elections remains intact at all levels of government.
Reinforcing the Connection Between Citizenship and Voting
Voting is the cornerstone of self-governance, and the right to vote is among the most sacred rights granted by citizenship. By limiting voting rights to U.S. citizens only, these LDs reinforce the importance of citizenship as a shared bond that ties individuals to the responsibilities of our democratic system. Opening elections to non-citizens undermines this bond and diminishes the value of citizenship, a principle that should remain central to Maine's democratic process.
Protecting Election Integrity and Public Confidence
Including non-citizens in elections creates unnecessary confusion and undermines public confidence in the electoral system. Voting rights for non-citizens blur the lines of accountability and loyalty to the state and nation. A recent survey by the Pew Research Center found that over 40% of voters were not confident that those who are ineligible to vote would be stopped from doing so.1 Regardless of one's feelings on the validity of those beliefs, we must fight the growing distrust in the democratic process in our country, and this bill is a great way to do that.
1
https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2024/10/24/confidence-in-voting-access-and-integrity-expectations-for-wheth er-and-when-the-election-results-will-be-clear/

Even Maine's Secretary of State Shenna Bellows has said that accusations of noncitizen voting that, in her view, are unsubstantiated still decrease public trust in our elections and even lay the groundwork to challenge future election results.2 Secretary Bellows is absolutely right; therefore, it is in Maine's best interest to cut off these claims before they even begin, and this is the best way to do it.
Localities are potentially undermining the citizenship requirement of voting.
Some localities, such as Portland, have been undermining the public trust in elections by considering allowing noncitizens to vote in local elections.3 The risk this poses is confusing a population that disproportionately knows English only as a second language and may be unaware of federal or state voting requirements. The Migration Policy Institute found that 56.4% of noncitizens in the United States spoke English less than "very well."4
Additionally, while Maine state law (21-A M.R.S.A. �111.1) currently disallows citizen voting, there is still some question as to whether our state home rule provisions allow circumventing this statute.5 Clarifying this rule by cementing it in the state constitution will avoid confusion for municipalities and noncitizens attempting to vote in the future.
Therefore, considering the confusion that different-level elections and a patchwork of local election rules can create for new arrivals to the country, this proposal would also help noncitizens avoid risking the accidental violation of state or federal law.
Conclusion
These bills are about ensuring fairness, transparency, and consistency in Maine's elections. By reserving the right to vote exclusively for U.S. citizens, this resolution strengthens our democratic system and preserves the sanctity of Maine's electoral process. Maine Policy Institute urges the committee to vote "Ought to Pass" on LDs 175 and 1437, reaffirming Maine's commitment to protecting the democratic rights of its citizens. Thank you for your time and consideration.

Testimony of Mayor of the City of Portland, Mark Dion
Before Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee
In Opposition to LD 1437, Resolution Proposing an Amendment to the Constitution of Maine to Specify
That Only Citizens May Vote in Elections
April 25, 2025
Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and honorable members of the Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee, I write to you on behalf of the City of Portland to express our opposition to LD 1437, a proposed amendment to the Constitution of Maine that would explicitly state that only citizens may vote in elections.
This resolution is unnecessary, redundant, and risks fostering confusion and exclusion at a time when trust in democratic institutions is already strained. The Maine Constitution and Maine law already clear - only United States citizens are eligible to vote.[1] LD 1437 does not change any existing legal rights or protections. Rather, the proposal introduces language that may be perceived as divisive or inflammatory, particularly toward immigrant communities.
Portland is a city that values civic engagement, inclusion, and trust in public institutions. Like many other parts of Maine, Portland is home to a diverse and growing population, including many immigrants and refugees who are integral to our workforce, economy, and cultural fabric. While they may not yet have full voting rights, these residents contribute significantly to the life of our city and often aspire to full civic participation as future citizens.

We respectfully urge the Committee to reject LD 1437 and instead focus legislative energy on policies that expand civic access, protect voting rights, and strengthen Maine's democratic institutions for all. JOINT STANDING COMMITTEE ON VETERANS AND LEGAL AFFAIRS

Testimony of Shenna Bellows, Secretary of State Department of the Secretary of State

May 2, 2025

Testifying In Opposition to

L.D. 1437, "RESOLUTION, Proposing an Amendment to the Constitution of Maine to Specify the
Qualifications of Electors in State and Local Elections"

Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans
and Legal Affairs, my name is Shenna Bellows, I reside in Manchester, and I am the Secretary of State and chief elections officer in Maine. I am speaking today in opposition to L.D. 1437.
Everyone agrees only citizens should vote in state and federal elections. I oppose L.D. 1437 because non-citizen voting is already prohibited under the Maine Constitution and by federal and state law. L.D. 1437 has been introduced based on a lie that non-citizen voting is a problem in our elections that
needs resolving. For these reasons this type of proposal has been voted down by the Legislature before, and I would encourage you all to vote against it again.
Article II of the Maine Constitution outlines the qualifications of electors, specifying that only citizens are eligible to vote in elections for Governor, Senators and Representatives. This is reiterated in the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, which was signed into law by
then-President Bill Clinton. And in Maine law, Title 30-A, (which governs local elections) section
2501 provides that the qualifications for voting in a municipal election conducted under that Title are governed solely by Title 21-A, section 111. Title 21-A, section 111 requires that the person voting must be a citizen of the United States. Non-citizens are already clearly barred from voting in Maine
elections �
The lie of noncitizen voting ~ either as something that is allowed and as something that is prevalent -- has persisted for many years now. But it is just that: a lie. According to Sean Morales-Doyle of the Brennan Center for Justice, "It amounts to a vanishingly rare phenomenon that is not going to impact the outcome of our elections in any real way, and where the people who actually are violating the law
are held accountable. Both domestic and foreign folks are spreading these lies in order to undermine faith in American elections -- some of them with the hope of overturning the result if they're not happy
about it."

I01 State House Station, Augusta, Maine 04333-010] www.Maine.gov/sos/cec," tel. 207-624~7736

Although thankfully we did not see the same efforts to overturn the results of the 2024 election as we did with the 2020 election, we should not pass a constitutional amendment based on a lie to placate those who would spread it or lay that groundwork. Returning members of this committee from two legislatures ago may recall testimony provided by
Mufalo Chitam of the Maine Immigrants' Rights Coalition. In her testimony, Ms. Chitam urged the committee not to pass a bill that capitalizes on anti-immigrant fervor. I echo that sentiment today and urge you to oppose this bill again this year.
For these reasons, we oppose L.D. 1437. Thank you and I would be happy to answer any questions that the committee may have.
